rv.q: So it is no surprise that the Metropolitan Opera’s impressive and enjoyable, if not quite crushing, first production of the work, which opened the company’s season on Tuesday, was anchored by an impressive and enjoyable, if not quite crushing, performance by the soprano Sondra Radvanovsky.
However, the opera itself, even in this eye-catching new production directed and designed by David McVicar, is a creaky thing.
All of it makes for a brilliant night at the opera starring an angry woman with a voice for the ages.
This was Medea's (and Radvanovsky’s) show, and in the end, she burned the house and the mirror to the ground, taking everyone but Giasone with her.
Overall, though, one cannot escape the sense of witnessing a historical relic, a feeling reinforced by David McVicar’s opulent but inert production...
Opera doesn’t get much better than this.
"Medea" is the first must-see production of the Met Opera's 2022-23 season.
The whole score resonated with a stature I’d never really appreciated.
Medea may or may not be a winner at the end but Radvanovsky, her colleagues, the Metropolitan Opera and Cherubini’s opera itself emerged as winners on opening night.
This is far and away Radvanovsky’s most audacious and compelling interpretation in her two decades-plus history at the Met.
Responding as a rap was a risk I chose to take But just like this Medea, I don’t think it’s a mistake.
Despite the opera’s flaws, The Met’s new production did justice by Cherubini and Medea .

cn.t: Radvanovsky earns ovations in the Met's long-overdue Medea debut, with critics largely praising her fierce performance. McVicar's production draws more divided responses, but the soprano's commanding presence wins the night.
